Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 114, verses 1–6:

Meccan, though it is said to be Medinan, and its verses number 6. [It was revealed after Surah al-Falaq.] In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

It is read as *qul a'udhu*, with the hamza of *a'udhu* dropped and its vowel transferred to the lam, and the like. So take four. [[Mahmud said: "If you ask, why did He attribute His name specifically to them, when He is the Lord of everything…etc." Ahmad said: In singling them out, he followed the usual practice of seeking compassion, for it is more complete with it. Back to his words. He said: "Malik an-nas" (the King of mankind) is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayān) to "Rabb an-nas" (the Lord of mankind). Or both are explicative appositions to the first, and the second is clearer, because "malik an-nas" may be applied to other than Allah, the Exalted, but "ilah an-nas" (the God of mankind) is applied only to Him, the Mighty and Majestic. So it is made the final point of clarification, and the clarification is increased by the repetition of the noun explicitly rather than by a pronoun. And Allah, glory be to Him, knows best. This is what Allah has facilitated of speech." I disassociate myself before Allah, the Exalted, from power and strength, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah bless our master Muhammad, and his family and companions, and grant them peace.]] Lord of mankind, with the attribution specifically to mankind? I say: because seeking refuge occurs from the evil of the whisperer who whispers into the breasts of mankind. It is as if it were said: I seek refuge from the evil of the whisperer who slips into mankind, by the Lord of mankind, who rules over their affairs, and who is their God and object of worship, just as some clients call upon their master when a calamity befalls them, their lord and the one who rules their affairs.

If you ask: "Malik an-nas, ilah an-nas": are they not from the Lord of mankind? I say: they are explicative appositions, like your saying: "the biography of Abu Hafs Umar al-Faruq." The first is clarified by "malik an-nas," then it is further clarified by "ilah an-nas," because the term "lord of mankind" may be said of others, as in His words ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ (9:31). And "malik an-nas" may also be said. But "ilah an-nas" is exclusive, with no partner in it, so it is made the final point of clarification. If you ask: why not suffice with mentioning the thing attributed to, which is "an-nas," just once? I say: because the explicative apposition is for clarification, so it calls for explicit mention rather than a pronoun.

Al-waswas is a noun meaning the whispering, like az-zilzal meaning the earthquake. As for the verbal noun, it is waswas with a kasra, like zilzal. What is meant by it is Satan, who is named by the verbal noun as if he were whispering in himself, because whispering is his craft and occupation, to which he is devoted. Or what is meant is "the one possessed of whispering." Al-waswasa is a hidden sound, and from it comes the rustle of jewelry.

Al-khannas is one who is accustomed to withdrawing, and is derived from al-khunus, which means to withdraw, like al-ʿawaj and al-battat. [[His words "like al-ʿawaj and al-battat": bayʿ al-ʿaj (seller of ivory), and bayʿ al-butut, which is a kind of garment. (ʿ)]] This is based on what is related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr: when a person remembers his Lord, Satan withdraws and turns away, and when he is heedless, he whispers to him. Alladhi yuwaswisu (who whispers) may take the three vowel cases in its position: the genitive, as an adjective, and the nominative and accusative as a reproach. It is good for the reader to pause at al-khannas and begin with alladhi yuwaswisu on one of these two readings. From the jinn and mankind: an explanation of alladhi yuwaswisu, on the basis that Satan is of two kinds: jinn and human, as He said ﴿the devils of mankind and jinn﴾ (6:112). And Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, said to a man: "Did you seek refuge with Allah from the Satan of mankind?" It is also permissible for min (from) to be connected to yuwaswisu, and its meaning is the starting point, i.e., he whispers into their breasts from the direction of the jinn and from the direction of mankind. It is also said: "from the jinn and mankind" is an explanation of "mankind." The name "mankind" applies to the jinn. They relied on the mention of a group of men and men in Surah al-Jinn. How worthy of verification is this! The jinn are called "jinn" because they are hidden (ijtinan), and mankind are called "nas" because they are visible, from al-inas, which means seeing, just as they are called "bashar" (human beings). If "mankind" applied to both groups, and that were correct and established, it would not fit the eloquence of the Qur'an, nor be free from artificiality. A better interpretation is that "mankind" means "those who forget" (al-nasi), like His words ﴿the day the caller calls﴾ (54:6), as is also read in ﴿from where the people (al-nas) pour forth﴾ (2:199). Then it is clarified by "the jinn and mankind," because the two weighty creatures are the two kinds described as forgetting the right of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Two surahs have been revealed to me, the like of which have not been revealed, and you will never read two surahs more beloved or more pleasing to Allah than these two." [[I have not found it with this wording. Its beginning in Muslim, in meaning, is from the hadith of ʿUqba ibn ʿAmir, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Have you not seen verses that were revealed tonight, the like of which has never been seen: Say, I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak; and Say, I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind." Its end is in Ibn Hibban from the hadith of ʿUqba, in meaning. And also he said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "A surah that is more beloved to Allah and more eloquent than Say, I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak and Say, I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind: if you can, do not leave them out of your prayer, then do so."]] He means the two protective surahs (al-muʿawwidhatayn). The two are also called al-muqashqishatan (the two that cleanse).

Abdullah, the one in need of Him, said: I seek refuge in them both, and in all the perfect and complete words of Allah, and I take shelter in the shelter of His comprehensive and universal mercy, from everything that wounds the religion, damages certainty, leads to regret in the end, or impairs faith that is mixed with flesh and blood. [[His words "mixed with flesh and blood" (al-masut bi-l-lahm wa-l-dam): i.e., mixed. This is what al-Sihah conveys. (ʿ)]] I ask Him, with humility of the neck, lowering of the gaze, and placing the cheek in the dust before His supreme and greatest majesty, seeking intercession with Him through His light, which is the gray hair in Islam, and seeking a means through repentance that purifies sins, and through what I have aspired to through my migration to Him and my settling near Him, and my perseverance in Mecca and my patience, despite weakness of strength and feebleness of steps. Then I ask Him by the truth of His straight path and His glorious, noble Qur'an, and by what I have endured of toil of the right hand and sweat of the brow, in the work of al-Kashshaf (the Unveiler) of its realities, releasing it from its difficulties, clarifying its obscurities, establishing it in its refutations, summarizing its subtleties and the refinements of its composition, drawing out its treasures and jewels of knowledge, filled with rare benefits found only in it, encompassing what cannot be fully grasped of its novel words and meanings, with brevity that removes superfluities and avoids what is disliked and tiresome. Even if its content contained nothing but placing each thing in its proper rule, it would suffice as a lost thing sought by scholars and a jewel desired by those who dive deep into the seas. And by what He honored me with and glorified me, and singled me out with His generosity and made me unique: through its elevation at my hands in the place of descent of its good tidings and warnings, and the place of revelation of its verses and surahs, in the secure city in the midst of the Sacred Precinct, and before the Sacred House, until the interpretation occurred, when the revelation was found: that He grant me a good ending, preserve me from a bad death, overlook my lapses on the Day of Mutual Loss, not disgrace me with them before the assembled witnesses, and settle me in the abode of permanence through His grace, by the breadth of His bounty and the abundance of His gift. Indeed, He is the Most Generous, the Most Kind, the Most Merciful.

(In a copy there is what follows:) In the author's own handwriting, may Allah have mercy on him: this copy is the first original copy, transcribed from the draft, and it is the blessed Harami copy of al-Kashshaf, sought for blessing, deserving that the blessings of heaven be drawn down by it and rain be sought through it in the year of drought. The author finished it with his hand facing the Kaaba, in the wing of his Sulaymaniyya house, which is at the gate of Ajyad, known as the School of the Scholar, in the forenoon of Monday, the twenty-third of Rabi al-Akhir, in the year five hundred and twenty-eight, and he was praising Allah for His manifest generosity, and sending blessings upon His servant and messenger, and upon his family and all his companions.
